name: Southwest Gully

waypoints.name: Easy Pass Trailhead
waypoints.note: Self-issue Northwest Forest Pass kiosk at the lot; NPS backcountry permit required for any overnight camping past the pass, and no potable water here.
waypoints.directions: From Marblemount, drive SR-20 (North Cascades Highway) east about 45 miles and turn right between mileposts 151 and 152 onto the short spur signed for Easy Pass, ending at a lot for about 10 cars. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass is required (self-issue at the kiosk). The highway closes in winter, so the trailhead is reachable only once it opens for the season.

waypoints.name: Granite Creek footlog crossing
waypoints.note: Trail crosses Granite Creek on a footlog roughly 300 yards from the trailhead, the last reliable low-elevation water before the climb to the pass.
waypoints.directions: Barely five minutes of level walking from the lot; the climbing does not begin until the far bank.

waypoints.name: Easy Pass
waypoints.note: Maintained trail tops out here; leave it before it drops toward Fisher Creek and sidehill south below Ragged Ridge at ~6,600-6,700 ft toward the Mesahchie/Katsuk basins.
waypoints.directions: From the far bank the trail climbs steadily for about three and a half miles and 2,900 ft — roughly two miles of hemlock and silver fir, then open avalanche meadows with three crossings of Easy Pass Creek before the final pitch to the notch. The upper section holds steep snow well into July and is worth an ice axe in early season. Figure two to three hours.

waypoints.name: Waterfall scree crossing
waypoints.note: Sidehill traverse is interrupted by a waterfall requiring a steep, loose 200-ft scree descent to get around/across it.
waypoints.directions: Drop over the far side toward Fisher Creek only as far as the end of the first switchback, where a faint climbers' path breaks off onto the ridge; it is unmarked and is the most commonly missed turn on the whole approach, and if you cannot find it, head for the ridge anyway. From there sidehill west across scree, talus, grass and blocky steps at around 6,600-6,800 ft. Take the waterfall low, on the easier bench a couple of hundred feet below the line you arrive on, rather than trying to force it at height.

waypoints.name: Basin camp south of Mesahchie Peak
waypoints.note: Established camp in a small basin marked by a rocky knob, below Mesahchie Col, roughly 5 hours off-trail from the trailhead.
waypoints.directions: Past the waterfall the traverse carries on west over more of the same loose sidehill into the basin, half a mile that eats far more time than the distance suggests. Flat ground is scarce, so take a site when you find one instead of pushing on for a better one.

waypoints.name: 7,400-ft bench above camp
waypoints.note: Gain the bench via 800 ft of class 3-4 climbing up ribs/gullies above camp, then traverse west toward the Grotesque Gendarmes.
waypoints.directions: Head west and up into the ribs and gullies directly above camp, picking the line by eye — there is no single correct one and the easiest way wanders. The rock is blocky and loose the whole way, so keep the party close and off each other's fall line.

waypoints.name: Grotesque Gendarmes traverse
waypoints.note: Technical crux of the approach: an exposed 250-300 ft descent scrambling past loose, blocky rock towers before the final gully.
waypoints.directions: Traverse west along the bench toward the low point between Katsuk and Kimtah, where the red rock towers stand. Losing height is unavoidable: the ground drops away as you scramble around and beneath them, and the exposure is genuine even though nothing on it is technically hard.

waypoints.name: Katsuk Peak summit
waypoints.note: Double summit (west/east peaks within about a foot of elevation); final pitch is class 3 granite up a gully with running water to the ridge crest just west of the true summit, then the class 4 summit block.
waypoints.directions: From beneath the last tower the gully is the obvious break leading back up to the crest, and entering the right one is the last real route-finding decision of the climb. Water runs in it low down, so expect wet rock and be careful where scree lies over slab. Anything knocked loose funnels straight onto whoever is below.

approach: Start at the Easy Pass Trailhead on SR-20 (milepost ~151, roughly 30 miles east of Newhalem / ~37 miles from Marblemount). Follow Easy Pass Trail (Green Trails Mt. Logan No. 49) 3.5-3.6 miles and about 2,700-3,000 ft of gain to Easy Pass at 6,550 ft — figure 2-3 hours. The trail crosses Granite Creek on a footlog near the start, climbs through about 2 miles of hemlock/silver-fir forest, then breaks into open avalanche meadows and crosses Easy Pass Creek three times before the final push to the pass; steep snow can linger on this upper section well into July and an ice axe is recommended into early summer. From the pass, drop down the North Cascades National Park side to the end of the first switchback, where a faint, easy-to-miss climbers' path breaks off onto Ragged Ridge — this junction is unmarked and is the most commonly botched route-finding point on the whole approach; if you don't spot the boot path, head off-trail toward the ridge anyway. From there, sidehill northwest across scree, talus, grass and blocky terrain at roughly 6,600-6,800 ft along the south side of the ridge (about an hour), crossing one notable waterfall/stream beneath Mesahchie Peak around 6,500 ft on an easy bench — this is the one water crossing of consequence on the traverse and also a reliable water source. Continue to the basin/shoulder at roughly 6,600-6,870 ft just south of the Katsuk-Mesahchie col, known as Ragged Ridge Camp (only two workable flat tent sites; good water draining the basin). An NPS backcountry permit is required to camp here. From camp, gain a further 200-600 ft to a saddle/bench on the ridge descending from Katsuk's west summit — tedious scree with a short stretch of 4th-class scrambling near the top — then locate the leftward-trending Southwest Gully high on the peak, which runs up toward a mushroom-shaped summit block. Low in the gully, bypass a waterfall by staying on its left (west) side on loose, 'kitty-litter' scree (Class 3). In early season (before roughly July) the entire gully holds steep snow to 45 degrees and demands an ice axe, crampons, and solid snow-climbing technique. Given the ~19.3 km round-trip distance, this is realistically an overnight approach (roughly 5 miles and about 3,000 ft to camp) rather than a single-push dayhike for most parties.
